claims.title: First Buddhist temples founded
claims.summary: Tibetan tradition credits King Songtsen Gampo with building the earliest Buddhist temples in the Bhutanese valleys, including Kyichu Lhakhang at Paro, as Buddhism spread south from Tibet.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies
sources.publisher: Federal Research Division, Library of Congress

claims.title: Guru Rinpoche brings Buddhism to Bhutan
claims.summary: The tantric master Guru Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) is said to have travelled into Bhutan, blessing sites such as Bumthang and the Taktsang cliff at Paro and marking the proper advent of Buddhism in the country.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies

claims.title: Drukpa Kagyu tradition takes root
claims.summary: The Drukpa ('Dragon') Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism spreads into the southern valleys and becomes the dominant religious tradition, lending Bhutan its name Druk Yul, the Land of the Thunder Dragon.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies
sources.publisher: Federal Research Division, Library of Congress

claims.title: Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal arrives in Bhutan
claims.summary: Fleeing a sectarian dispute in Tibet, the Drukpa Kagyu lama Ngawang Namgyal enters western Bhutan and is recognised as the Zhabdrung, beginning the unification of the country.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies
sources.publisher: Federal Research Division, Library of Congress

claims.title: Punakha Dzong founded
claims.summary: The Zhabdrung begins building Punakha Dzong at the confluence of two rivers as his capital, one of a network of fortress-monasteries that became the seats of Bhutan's temporal and religious power.

sources.label: Bhutan — Tentative List (Dzongs: the centre of temporal and religious authorities)

claims.title: Dual system of government established
claims.summary: The Zhabdrung institutes the chhoesi dual system, splitting power between a spiritual Je Khenpo and a secular Druk Desi; his death around this time is concealed to preserve the fledgling state.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies

claims.title: A Chinese imperial army enters Bhutan
claims.summary: Qing forces invade and briefly establish control — the first of three outside powers to reach into the valleys within two centuries.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Bhutan: The Land of the Thunder Dragon — from Guru Rinpoche's blessing to the world's first kingdom of Gross National Happiness.", terralore.co/country/BTN/chronicle#ev-1720-a-chinese-imperial-army-enters-bhutan, claim TL:BTN:event:1720:a-chinese-imperial-army-enters-bhutan, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The first British intervention
claims.summary: A century before the Duar War, British forces intervene in Bhutan — the beginning of the Raj's long pressure on its southern frontier.

claims.title: The Duar War with British India
claims.summary: After a failed British mission and disputes over the southern duars, Britain and Bhutan fight a five-month war that ends in Bhutanese defeat.

claims.title: Treaty of Sinchula
claims.summary: Bhutan cedes the Bengal and Assam duars to British India in exchange for an annual subsidy, fixing its modern southern border and binding it to the Raj.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies

claims.title: Treaty of Punakha
claims.summary: Revising the Sinchula terms, Britain increases Bhutan's subsidy and pledges non-interference in internal affairs while guiding its foreign relations, securing Bhutan's continued independence.

sources.label: Friendship and International Relations in the Himalayas: Bhutan, Britain, and the 1910 Treaty of Punakha

claims.title: Ugyen Wangchuck crowned first king
claims.summary: An assembly at Punakha Dzong unanimously elects Ugyen Wangchuck, penlop of Tongsa, as the first hereditary Druk Gyalpo, ending the dual system and founding the Wangchuck dynasty.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies

claims.title: Accession of the second king
claims.summary: On Ugyen Wangchuck's death the crown passes peacefully to his son Jigme Wangchuck, confirming the stability of the new hereditary monarchy.

sources.label: Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies

claims.summary: Delhi guarantees non-interference in Bhutan's internal affairs while retaining influence over its foreign relations — the terms of British Punakha, inherited by a new republic.

claims.title: National Assembly established
claims.summary: King Jigme Dorji Wangchuck creates the Tshogdu, Bhutan's National Assembly, beginning the reform of the country's institutions alongside the abolition of serfdom and land redistribution.

claims.summary: Bhutan is admitted as the 128th member of the United Nations, a milestone in its emergence from isolation and its assertion of full sovereignty.

claims.title: Gross National Happiness proclaimed
claims.summary: On acceding to the throne, the young fourth king Jigme Singye Wangchuck advances Gross National Happiness as Bhutan's guiding measure of development, valuing well-being and culture over GDP alone.

claims.title: Slavery abolished
claims.summary: The third king abolishes slavery and serfdom, one of the first acts of a reign that would open a closed kingdom deliberately and slowly.

claims.title: The first foreign tourists
claims.summary: Bhutan admits its first tourists — a controlled opening, priced and permitted rather than free, and still the model today.

claims.title: The census and the citizenship rules
claims.summary: A census brands many ethnic Nepalis illegal immigrants, and measures stressing Tibetan-derived Bhutanese culture antagonise the Lhotshampa; violent unrest follows in the south in 1990.

claims.title: Exodus of the Lhotshampa
claims.summary: Amid 'one nation, one people' measures and stricter citizenship rules, tens of thousands of southern Bhutanese of Nepali origin leave or are expelled, and more than 100,000 end up in UNHCR camps in eastern Nepal.

claims.title: Resettlement of Bhutanese refugees
claims.summary: A multinational programme led by UNHCR and IOM resettles over 100,000 Bhutanese refugees from Nepal to countries including the United States, Canada, Australia and Europe.

claims.title: Television and the internet arrive
claims.summary: Limited television and internet services are permitted and several dozen political prisoners released, a decade after the kingdom tightened.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Bhutan: The Land of the Thunder Dragon — from Guru Rinpoche's blessing to the world's first kingdom of Gross National Happiness.", terralore.co/country/BTN/chronicle#ev-1999-television-and-the-internet-arrive, claim TL:BTN:event:1999:television-and-the-internet-arrive, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The treaty with India revised
claims.summary: A new agreement gives Bhutan more say over its own foreign and defence policy, loosening a constraint carried from 1910 through 1949.

claims.title: Constitution and democratic monarchy
claims.summary: Following the country's first parliamentary elections, Bhutan's written Constitution comes into force, transforming the kingdom into a democratic constitutional monarchy with Gross National Happiness as a goal of the state.

claims.title: Coronation of the fifth king
claims.summary: Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck is formally enthroned as the fifth Druk Gyalpo, his coronation timed to the centenary of the Wangchuck monarchy and the inauguration of democratic rule.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Bhutan: The Land of the Thunder Dragon — from Guru Rinpoche's blessing to the world's first kingdom of Gross National Happiness.", terralore.co/country/BTN/chronicle#ev-2008-coronation-of-the-fifth-king, claim TL:BTN:event:2008:coronation-of-the-fifth-king, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: A prime minister questions Gross National Happiness
claims.summary: Tshering Tobgay says the concept is overused and masks real problems — rising debt, chronic unemployment, poverty and corruption.
